THE FIFTH DISTRICT CONTEST.

THE FIFTH DISTRICT CONTEST.
Special to the Gazette.

PITTSBURG, TEX., Aug. 25.—The Fifth judicial convention was called to order by Chairman C. S. Todd at 1:30 p. m. The ballot stood: Baldwin 15 and O'Neil 13. The number of ballots taken is 1201, Baldwin leading in all.

In the executive committee for the Fifth district, which was elected to-day, Baldwin's men selected their men, and are as follows- P. Turner of Bowie, chairman; Ben Athiker of Bowie, J. F. Reynolds of Camp, R. D. Lockett of Cass, J. B. Stringer of Franklin, J. M. Tncker of Marion: J. M. Moore of Morrs, George Conty of Titus. The convention adjourned until to-night at 8:30.

COME HOME TO CHANGE CLOTHES.
Special to the Gazette.

TEXARKANA, TEX., Aug. 25.—The Bowie county delegates returned this morning to the Pittsburg judicial convention, which failed last week to make a nomination. The delegation, some twenty in number, came home for their better clothes and declare that they will ballot if necessary until the November election. It will be remembered that this county instructed for O'Neill.

Grand preparations are being made to receive Governor Eagle of Arkansas, who will arrive some time to-night and speak to the people on the East Side tomorrow. Fizer, his opponent, will also speak.

REPUBLICAN CONVENTION BROKEN UP. Special to the Gazette.

THURBER, TEX., Aug. 25.—Our people here and all over the county have been considerably stirred up for the past few days over an outrage perpetrated by the hoodlum element of Dublin against four delegates from this place to the Republican convention which was to have convened at Dublin on the 16th inst. It seems that as soon as it was known that a couple of negroes were among the delegates the darklantern clans began to collect their forces and organize for the purpose of running the negroes out and breaking up the Republican convention. The delegates from this place received their "orders" and returned home as fast as their teams would bring them and the convention was broken up. Our best citizens condem this infamous outrage and the Republicans of the county are earnestly invited to hold their convention at Stephenville where they will have every protection and be treated with every courtesy. From the best information obtained the men who engaged in such shameful conduct at Dublin belong to the political class called the darklanternites.

SAN ANTONIO'S LILY WHITES.

Special to the Gazette.

SAN ANTONIO, TEX., Aug. 25.—The white Republicans of San Antonio, known locally as the 'Lily Whites,' who were badly downed by the legs at the Mission Garden massmeeting Saturday night, are restive.

They circulated a call for another mass meeting to-day, and will probably get together to-morrow. When they do they will elect another set of delegates to the county convention. The leaders of the movement are James R. Newcomb, B. F. Johnson, of the Light, A. P. Tugwell and some others of the prominent white Republicans of the county. There will be excessively savage and amusing warfare in the county convention, which in all probability will be carried into the state convention.

HOUSTON REPUBLICANS.

Special to the Gazette.

HOUSTON, TEX., Aug. 25.—Caucuses among Republicans are in order. They want Col. John T. Brady to run against Stewart for congress, but the colonel is too wise, and they are to-night looking or a man to lead their forlorn hope.

A SPLIT IN UNION LABOR RANKS.

St. Louis, Mo., Aug. 25.—A dispatch from Jefferson City says what is known as the Garland companion wing of the Union Labor party met in state convention this morning with thirty-four delegates present, all from St. Louis. E. L. Briggs was elected temporary chairman, and after the appointment of the usual committees the convention adjourned until 3 p. m.

A factional fight in the party is apt to give the secretary of state some trouble. Under the Australian ballot the party must poll 3 per cent. of the vote of the state before it is entitled to present candidates for state officers. The vote polled at the last election (19,000) barely permitted of this. Now there is a split in the party, and two conventions have been called, and it is supposed that two sets of tickets, each claiming to be the regular Union Labor ticket, be nominated. Between these two tickets the secretary of the defeated faction will likely resort to mandamus proceeding, and in this event the constitutionality of the law itself will be passed upon.

Upon reassembling at 3 o'clock the report of the committee on credentials was heard and permanent organization effected.

W. H. Garland was elected chairman and John T. Davis, secretary. A state committee was named and the executive committee declared abolished.

The convention then adjourned until 7 o'clock, at which time committees on platform and resolutions will render their reports.

The Report that Republicans were Driven Out of the City Indignantly Denied. DUBLIN, Tex., Aug. 27, 1890.

DUBLIN, Tex., Aug. 27, 1890.
Editor Gazette.
Seeing in your valuable paper of the 26th a report from Thurber in regard to a Republican convention that was to have met here on Saturday the 16th, but which failed to materialize on account of the fact that two colored delegates arrived here on the Rio Grande train the night previous, were by some irresponsible parties ordered to leave town, but not on account of their politics, but their color. Had it been known in time they (the delegates), would have been protected by the best citizens of our city, and to make this fact more plain at a mass meeting of the citizens held on Friday last the following preamble and resolutions were adopted, and as seen were indorsed by the leading Republicans of our city:
Whereas, we the citizens of Dublin, believing that the constitution of the United States guarantees to every man freedom of thought, freedom of speech and the utmost liberty, social and political, consistent with the welfare of our institu tions, we deplore the action of one or two persons whereby those who came here upon a political mission were led to misunderstand our sentiments and mistake the action of one or two as the sentiment of our citizens generally; therefore be it Resolved, 1. That the sentiment expressed

THE FULL FACTS.
The Erath County Republican Convention no. t Held at Dublin on Account of the small turn Out.
Hot SPRINGS, ARK., Aug. 27, 1890.

In your issue of the 26th inst. appears an article from Thurber, Tex., which reflects on the good citizens and peace officers of Dublin, Tex. As a law abiding citizen and mayor of the city of Dublin, Tex., please allow me space to correct the false statement made by the author of the communication from Thurber, who did not have nerve enough to sign his name to the article referred to. It is true there were two negro delegates from Thurber to the Republican county convention which was to convene in the city of Dublin on the 16th inst., and when they (the negro delegates) went up town from the Fort Worth and Rio Grande depot there were one or two irresponsible persons who told the negro delegates that they had better "git," that they did not want any Republican convention in Dublin. The matter was immediately reported to me. I met Mr. Arthur Miller and Mr. Ed Pierson, the two white gentlemen that came over with the two negro delegates from Thurber. We called on G. N. Arnold, a respected citizen of Dublin and chairman of the Erath county Republican executive committee, and we together went to the negro delegates and I and Mr. Arnold prevailed on them to stay. I told them repeatedly that they should be protected in every respect. Mr. Arnold and myself also plead with Messrs. Miller and Pierson not to leave, knowing that if they did leave under such circumstances there would be a big bloody shirt wave over the matter, which was uncalled for. As to the two white delegates receiving orders to leave the city, it was absolutely false. There was but one white delegate from Thurber, Mr. Arthur Miller being a staunch Democrat. Mr. Ed Pierson was a white delegate from Thurber and a nice gentleman and one of Erath county's old and respected citizens.

On the morning of the 16th instant other delegates began to come in from other portions of the county, there being all told only twelve or fifteen, it my memory serves me right. I together with several other citizens called on Chairman Arnold to learn what time the convention would be called together. Chairman Arnold and others said that they had about decided not to hold any convention on account of being such a poor turnout. 1, with other citizens, prevailed on Chairman Arnold to hold the convention, but they finally decided not to have any convention, not on account of the little matter arising over the negro delegates, not because they were afraid, not because they did not have protection under the law, but for reasons above stated.

If the Republicans of Erath county are disposed to recall a county convention they are cordially invited to reassemble in Dublin. The good citizens will welcome them and make them feel at home without Stephenville as a body guard. R. H. McCain, Mayor of the city of Dublin.

Policeman Hogue, in attempting to quell the disturbance, had a scuffle with Jones. The officer drew a pistol and fired three times at Jones in quick succession, the last shot proving fatal. Some feeling was exhibited among the negroes at the killing of Jones. Mrs. S. A. H. Terry Beaten Again.
SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 2.—Mrs. Sarah Althea Terry had a retrial of her case against the estate of the late Senator Sharon in the Superior Court, and Judge Shafter yesterday rendered a decision holding that the so-called marriage contract was a forgery; that she never had been married to Sharon, and had no claim whatever upon the Sharon estate.

SHOT IN THE STREET. JULIAN JONES, COLORED, SHOT BY OFFICER HOGUE. An Obstreperous Negro Knocks Down Three Men, Resists an Officer and is Shot Down---He Lives Only a Short While.
Two pistol shots in sharp, quick succession on Hargett street startled all that portion of the city yesterday afternoon about 4 o'clock. The two reports were followed in a few seconds by another shot and a negro man was seen to fall. A person passing up Fayetteville street at that time would have seen a little way up Hargett street, about in front of D. T. Johnson's store, an excited commotion, with people running in all directions and getting behind trees to avoid the pistol shots. Then a tall, gaunt, slender wiry negro, apparently about forty-five years of age, with a little gray in his hair was seen rushing toward Fayetteville Street with officer William E. Hogue following close on his heels with a pistol in his hand. At the third shot the negro wavered and seemed about to fall and Policeman Hogue grasped him. He was on the point of shooting him again when he saw that he had already struck him and that he was about to fall.

GOT INTO A DIFFICULTY.

The negro man was Julian Jones, and he lives in the country, and works on Mr. Goodwin's farm, known as the Upchurch farm. He came to town yesterday, and imbibed pretty freely of intoxicants during the day.

Yesterday evening Jones got into a difficulty with a white man named Tom Frazier, who lives in St. Mary's township. The difficulty occurred in front of Miss Woodard's dry goods store on Wilmington street. Jones knocked Mr. Frazier down, and was pummeling him when Mr. William Utley arrived on the scene, and rushed up and endeavored to pull Jones off. Jones then turned and struck Mr. Utley a sledge-hammer lick which made him dizzy and came near taking him off his feet. When he sufficiently recovered he started toward the negro who ran around the corner. About this time officer Hogue saw the trouble and ran up just as Mr. Utley caught up with Jones on Hargett street. Jones then turned and struck at Mr. Utley but officer Hogue rushed in and ATTEMPTED TO ARREST JONES, and he struck him instead, felling him to his knees. As soon as the officer recovered himself he attempted to get the use of his club, which he had swung to his left wrist by a strap. He attempted to change it to his right hand, and as he did so the negro snatched it from him. A scuffle ensued, in which the billy was dropped, but officer Hogue tried to get it in vain. He then drew his pistol, whereupon the negro started to run and officer Hogue

FIRED AT HIM TWICE.

He was close upon him and caught him and fired a third time. He was on the point of firing again when Jones fell.

Officer Hogue had lost both his hat and his club in the scuffle with the negro and these were about this time brought up to him.

A dense crowd soon collected and it was found necessary to take Jones into the rear of the store. He was taken into the rear lot and physicians were at once summoned. The examination revealed the fact that a ball had entered his side above the left hip and passed into the abdomen. It was difficult to find a physician and was fully twenty-five minutes after the shooting when

DOCTORS HINES AND GOODWIN both arrived about the same time. Jones said nothing from the time he was shot except to groan and mutter and roll and toss as if in great pain. Dr. Hines had scarcely looked at him a moment before he said: "Nothing can be done for that man, he is done for." It was evident that he was in the throes of death and he soon breathed his last.

OFFICER HOGUE talked freely when interviewed and stated the main facts of the occurrence about as above. He said: I did not shoot until I had been struck and disarmed of my club and when I thought it was necessary to do so to make the arrest. I am heartily sorry to have killed the man and would not have done so if it could have been avoided."

Jones, it is understood, was drinky and had been creating considerable disturbance. He is said to be a good negro when sober, but when he is drinking becomes wild and crazy and uncontrollable. He is tall, wiry and angular, with sharp, thin cut features and piercing eyes. He is well known around town and is said to be 45 years old.

The testimony of the defense brought out the fact that after officer Hogue fired the first two shots which are supposed to have missed Jones, the latter halted and the officer came up and took hold of him when he

AGAIN TURNED UPON HIM and struck him. Then the officer shot him the third and fatal shot.

He stated that he was standing in his door when he saw the commotion and saw Jones running down the street with Hogue after him and heard the first two shots fired. The other witnesses for the defense were Messrs. W. M. Utley, Geo. F. Kennedy, R. P. Finch, E. G. Horton. Frank Redford and O. W. Belvin. After hearing argument Justice Barbee announced that he would postpone judgment till tomorrow at 12 o'clock when it is probable that some additional argument will be made and the judgment of the court as to whether the case is one of murder or manslaughter, upon which will depend admission to bail will be given. Policeman Hogue is in the meantime in the custody of the sheriff.

There was considerable expression of feeling heard on the part of the negroes but there seemed to be no trouble imminent.

NORTH CAROLINA NEWS
EXCITING :SHOOTING AFFRAY IN RALEIGH.
Negro Killed While Resisting an Officer—Another Alliance Defeat in Congressional Convention—Items of Interest From Many Points.
RALEIGH, N. C., Aug. 2.—[Special.]—A sensation was created here this afternoon by a tragedy which occurred on one of the principal streets. Julien Jones, a negro who lives near the city, got into a difficulty with a white man named Tom Frazin, and knocked him down. Mr. William Utley, formerly editor of the Evening Visitor of this city, happened to be near by, and went up and attempted to pull the negro off of Frazin, whom he was still pounding. Jones thereupon struck Utley and knocked him down. At that moment Policeman Hogue attempted to arrest Jones, when he was also felled to his knees by a lick from the negro, who pounced upon him, took his club from him, and jumped up and started off. Hogue shot the negro three times. One ball penetrated his abdomen.

He fell to the sidewalk and died in a few minutes. Tremendous crowds of negroes, who are in the city by hundreds, gathered around, and were heard to murmer ominously about the affair, but were dispersed by the police, and it is not believed that any trouble will occur. Officer Hogue was placed under arrest, an investigation of the shooting was began.

After hearing witnesses, Justice Barbee postponed judgment till Monday morning, and Officer Hogue was committed to jail without bail. Justice Barbee did not render a decision as to whether the case was one of murder or manslaughter, but the general opinion prevails that his judgment will be the latter.

TRINITY COLLEGE.

The building committee of Trinity College met at Durham yesterday and decided to erect two buildings for the new college instead of one. Both will be elegant three-story structures.

FARMERS' ALLIANCE.

Yesterday, at Salisbury, the Farmers' Alliance met with their second defeat for the Congressional nomination. A hard flight has been made in that district between Hon. John S. Henderson, the present representative, and Hon. A. Leazar, the candidate of the Farmers' Alliance and Speaker of the House of Representatives of the present Legislature. The forces were marshaled yesterday with all the strength of both sides, and Henderson was nominated on the first ballot by a vote of 171 to 124.

A week ago, Hon. B. H. Bunn was nominated in this district, beating Strand, the Alliance candidate. Three of the old Democratic standard bearers in other districts have been forced, however, to withdraw, because they did not suit the Alliance, which has decided to take matters in hand, as it now appears. These three are Congressmen Rowland, Skinner and Simmons. It is estimated that six out of the twelve Congressmen from this State in the next Congress will be Alliance men.

RALEIGH ELECTRIC LIGHTS.

At a meeting of the Board of Aldermen of the city last night, a proposition was submitted to change the present electric are lights used for illuminating the present streets, from 1,200 candle-power to 2,000 candle-power. It is found to be necessary to increase the power of the lights, and the proposition will in all pr ability be adopted. The 2,000 candle-power lights are the strongest that are made.

NEGROES RESTIVE.

News is received here this morning of an imminent uprising of negroes at Rutherfordton, and great alarm is said to exist. The trouble grew out of a negroe's resisting an officer who was arresting him whereupon the officer shot the negro. The wound is feared to be fatal, and the negroes are reported to be much incensed.

JOHN ROBINSON'S SHORTCOMINGS.

A sensation has been created among the entire colored population of Durham by the shortcomings of one, John Robinson colored, who had charge of all the moneys and acts as treasurer for all the colored churches of the place.

He Assails a Police Officer and is Shot Dead.
[By telegraph to the Dispatch.]
RALEIGH, N. C., August 2.—This after

BY telegraph to the Dispatch.1
RALEIGH, N. C., August 2.—This afternoon a negro named Julian Jones had a difficulty with a white man on the principal business street here and knocked him down. Policeman Hogue called on William Utley, a well-known newspaper-man, to assist in quelling the disturbance. Jones knocked Utley down, and in a scuffle with Hogue got his club and was about to use it when the officer drew his pistol and fired three times at Jones in quick succession, the last shot proving fatal. One shot struck a clerk in a neighboring store in the leg. Some feeling was exhibited among the negroes at the killing of Jones.

PO LICE SENSATION. OFFICER HOGUE KILLS A MAN WHILE RESISTING ARREST.
Another: Man Accidentally Shot-- The Officer Jailed to Await the Result of an Investigation.

Raleigh had the biggest sensation and excitement yesterday she has experienced since the famous Boyle case.

Officer Hogue, of the police force, shot and killed a colored man named Julius Jones.

Hogue was trying to arrest the negro.

The trouble started on Wilmington street in front of Woodward's store. A white man named Bob Frazier and Jones were talking. Frazier cursed Jones. Jones struck Frazier and knocked him down, and had drawn back to strike again, when Mr. Wm. Utley, who happened to be standing by stepped forward and caught Jones' arm for the purpose of parting the men and preventing further trouble. Jones wheeled on Mr. Utley and struck him a terrific blow under the eye, knocking him backward. Then he broke and run.

Officer Hogue was on the street, south of the place where the trouble was going on. He saw the negro strike Mr. Utley and run, and started after him. Mr. Utley was also in pursuit. They were running northward toward Hargett street. Some parties report that the officer fired at the negro while running on Wilmington street, but the shot did not take effect. At the corner of Wilmington and Hargett street Mr. Utley caught the negro, and was in a scuffle with him when the officer arrested him. The negro turned and struck Mr. Hogue and then there was another scuffle during which the officer's billet dropped to the ground. Nobody seems to be able to tell which picked up the billet, but the negro broke from the officer and run again, up Hargett street towards Fayetteville. The officer gave chase and fired his pistol at him again.

This was a very bad and unfortunate shot. The ball struck Mr. Furman Betts, who was standing in the door of his father's grocery. It went into the thigh, inflicting an ugly and painful wound but not a dangerous one.

In the excitement prevailing no one noticed that Mr. Betts was shot. The officer still pursued the negro, and a few yards further on caught him again.

The reports of what occurred at this point from eye witnesses do not harmonize. The officer says the negro was showing fight, and that while he was scuffling with him he heard parties cry out, "shoot him, shoot him; he's got your billet." Then he placed the muzzle of the pistol against the negro's abdomen and fired. Jones fell over at once and the struggle, of course, was at an end.

Some eye witnesses say that the negro was not showing fight, but was trying to get away from Hogue, when he (Hogue) threw one arm around the negro to hold him, and with the other hand fired the fatal shot into his stomach.

A tremendous crowd congregated at the scene with lightning rapidity. It was almost impossible to get the wounded negro through it, but he was taken up and carried into an open court in the rear of Williams & Haywood's drug store.

Physicians were immediately summoned, the first one called being Dr. Hines. He came down to the scene, and some one directed him to go to Mr. Furman Betts who was suffering from his wound. Dr. Hines thought he had been called to attend Mr. Betts, and, stopping to dress his wounds, it was some time before he got to where Jones was. Dr. Goodwin came into the open court first, and Dr. Hines came directly afterward through another entrance. They examined the wounded man, and a moment afterward Dr. Hines said, "It's useless to try to do anything. The wound is fatal." A few minutes afterward the poor unfortunate colored man had breathed his last. After some consultation among the city authorities, it was decided that an inquest was unnecessary, and Jones' body was turned over to his friends who took it to his home on Goodwin's farm, near Ramkhatte, where he worked.

Officer Hogue Arrested.

Officer Hogue was in the open court with the fatally wounded man for some time, and showed great impatience at the delay in the arrival of the physician ans. He talked freely to the reporters who were present, but said he could not tell exactly how the matter occurred. He said he had become greatly excited in the melee and could not tell all the minutiae of what had happened. He could not tell whether or not in the first struggle, his billet had fallen to the ground, or whether Jones had gotten it. He said he was in the act of transferring it frhm his left to his right hand when Jones tried to get it; but he could not tell whether Jones knocked it from his hand to the ground, or had secured it.

He came out of the open court and walked up and down the street several times and then went to the Mayor's office.

Very soon after the shooting, a color man named William Jones went before M. B. Barbee and swore out a warrant for the arrest of Officer Hogue on a charge of murder. Deputy Newson served the warrant and arrested the officer in the Mayor's office.

After the arrest had been made, Justice Barbee came in and arrangement were made at once for a preliminary hearing.

Hogue in Jail Pending a Decision.

Justice Barbee called the case for hearing at a little after five o'clock, and the investigation continued without interruption until nearly ten o'clock.

Raleigh Swept the Deck.

The CHRONICLE maintains that Raleigh and vicinity is the best place for anything that can be found anywhere. The statement does'nt need any proof, but if it did there is always something occurring to prove it. The latest "sweep" for Raleigh was at the Mt. Holly fair. MORN WITNESSES Evidence Resumed in the Shooting Case---- Continued Till Today.
The preliminary trial of Police Officer Hogue was resumed yesterday at 12 o'clock at the court house instead of the Mayor's office, and at the hour appointed the room was well filled.

In resuming the case Justice Barbee stated that he desired to say that some facts had been stated in the newspapers which did not come before the court on Saturday night and that he thought it would be proper to re-open the evidence in order that any additional facts might come before the court if the parties interested desired it.

Mr. Devereux on the part of the prosecution said that the prosecution was not prepared to reply to newspaper rumors. Statements had been made in the newspapers which were not facts, that is not facts in evidence before the court.

The prosecution then introduced several witnesses in addition to those sworn on Saturday night.

Philip Harris, colored, was first examined. He testified that he was at Markham's corner on Saturday afternoon and saw the shooting. He saw Jones run around Woodard's corner and a white man after him with a stick. The policeman appeared on the other side of the street near Mabry's bar and was coming from Fayetteville street. He ran in and struck Jones with his billy. The policeman was then struck and fell to the ground and when he got up he got up shooting. He followed him on up the street shooting at him. Mr. J. N. Holding cross-examined the witness.

Nick Blount, colored, testified that he saw the shooting from the east side of Wilmington street. He saw Jones and a white man fighting and saw Hogue run up. Hogue did not strike Jones. Jones struck a lick at one of them and the policeman fell. The policeman then begun to fire. He saw the policeman catch Jones by the right arm and fire into his left side. Blount was cross-examined.

William Green, colored, said he was on Hargett street, near Williams & Haywood's drug store, with his wagon Saturday evening. Jones and an another man were fighting. He saw Hogue come up. He was some distance from Jones when he shot. Jones cried for somebody to help him, and Hogue said d—n you, I'll help you. It was the second shot that hit him, and when Hogue caught him he shot him again. On cross-examination Green said Jones was struck twice, by both the second and third shots.

Mr. R. T. Mills, white, was examined. He said he was in front of Crocker's store, on the north side of Hargett street, and saw the shooting as described, but heard nothing said.

Mr. C. O. Ball, white, said he was in front of his store on Hargett street Saturday evening. He saw the first two shots and the negro running. The negro stopped and turned toward Hogue just before the last shot.

Mr. Alvin Betts, merchant on Hargett street, said he was at his place of business when the shooting occurred. He was in the store, and heard the first two shots. His son, Mr. Furman Betts, who was standing in the door, exclaimed that he was shot.

THE PISTOL PRODUCED.

The pistol with which the shooting was done was then brought into court, and was identified by Officer Woodall as Officer Hogue's pistol. It is a 38-calibre, double action Smith and Wesson.

The prosecution announced that this concluded their testimony so far as they could tell, and that they would rest the case here.

The defense stated that they desired to introduce other witnesses who could not be produced till this morning and asked that the case be postponed till that time which after some discussion was agreed to. Proceedings were then suspended till 11 o'clock this morning and Officer Hogue was remanded to jail. During the proceedings the court room was densely packed, the crowd consisting mostly of colored people. The interest which centers in the case has not been surpassed by any recent event which has transpired in the city.

Dr. W. S. Black to Succeed Dr. Dixon.

The trustees of the Oxford Orphan Asylum have elected Rev. Dr. W. S. Black, of this city, Superintendent of the Asylum to succeed Dr. B. F. Dixon. Dr. Black has for years been presiding elder of the Raleigh District of the M. E. Conference and our people are warmly attached to him. With our congratulations to him and to Oxford go our deepest regrets at losing him from our midst.

RALEIGH.
Examination of Policeman Hogue Continued.
RALEIGH, N. C., Aug. 4. [Special.]

The preliminary investigation of Policeman Hogue for shooting Julien Jones, negro, on Saturday evening, was resumed this morning before Justice M. B. Barbee, and after the examination of several witnesses, the case was continued till tomorrow, in order that other witnesses may be summoned. Hogue in the mean time remained in jail. It was evident to-day that much feeling exists on the part of the negroes in regard to the affair. They deserted their work and docked to the trial by hundreds, and thronged the court-room.

Some were heard to talk openly in a threatening manner of what would be done if Hogue goes free. Trouble was apprehended late Saturday night, and the Governor's Guard was ordered under arms, and slept in their armory Saturday night and last night, to be in readiness in case of an outbreak. At all the negro churches in this city collections were taken up last night to employ attorneys to prosecute Hogue.

OXFORD ORPHAN ASYLUM.

Rev. Dr. W. S. Block, of this city, has been elected superintendent of Oxford Orphan asylum, to succeed Dr. B. F. Dixon. He is one of the most eminent divines in the North Carolina Conference, and has for years been presiding elder of Raleigh district.

RALEIGH.
Governor's Guard to Be Strengthened—
Fatal Drunken Row.
In view of bad blood which has been plainly shown by negroes here for several days past on account of the Hogue shooting affair, a special meeting of the Board of Aldermen was called last night and an appropriation of $150 was made to equip more fully and make more efficient the Governor's Guard of this city in order that company may be prepared for any emergency. In consequence of the intense feeling shown by negroes, Hogue's counsel have decided not to institute habeas corpus proceedings, but to allow him to remain in jail until trial.

Rev. Sam Jones has written a letter announcing that he will commence a series of meetings in Wilmington on September 25th, and will continue ten days or longer. Many doubted whether or not Mr. Jones would accept the invitation to go to Wilmington, as violent opposition to his coming has been expressed by some of the local ministers there.

On Tuesday, in Burke county, near Morganton, two men Dave and John Brittian, engaged in a fatal drunken row. The two men are cousins, and the fight grew out of a scuffle over a jug of liquor. Dave Brittian struck John with the jug in the face, cutting him tearfully, and then proceeded to pummel him with his fist. Another Brittian, who was present, pulled Dave off, and while he was holding him "John" attacked Dave with a knife, giving him several fearful wounds, one stroke of the knife making a hole in Dave's left side four or five inches in width, and cutting into the left lung. He lived only a shortwhile.

George Law, mate of the schooner James Ponder fell overboard and was drowned last night at Wilmington while climbing over the ship's side to go ashore.

Investigation of the recent murder of Sam Potter, in Greene county, has brought light the existence of White Caps in that neighborhood. One man testified to having received a letter on the day Potter was killed signed, "Captain of White Caps." Potter was an immoral and odious character, and had received two or three notices to leave. The wife of Sam Potter testified that on the night of the killing she and her husband had retired, but on hearing tiring her husband rose, dressed and armed himself contrary to her entreaties, and went in the direction of the firing. His body was found next morning completely riddled. It is announced that the Republicans of the Eighth Congressional district will put R. Z. Linney in the field as a Congressional candidate, and that he will carry on an aggressive canvass. Linney is an apostate Democrat who went over to the Republicans a few years ago.
